stem: The student wants to emphasize the bridge's engineering achievement relative to earlier thin-arch bridges. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Vella River Footbridge was completed in 1931 in the town of Kestrel Falls.
• Engineer Hana Dvořáková designed it with reinforced concrete arches only 9 centimeters thick.
• At the time, most concrete arch bridges of similar span used arches at least 30 centimeters thick.
• Thin concrete arches had been built earlier in Switzerland, but those bridges required steel cable supports.
• Dvořáková's bridge was the first to span more than 40 meters with a thin concrete arch and no cable supports.
• The bridge still carries pedestrians today.
choices: Completed in 1931, Hana Dvořáková's Vella River Footbridge, whose concrete arches are only 9 centimeters thick, still carries pedestrians across the river today.
Dvořáková's bridge was the first to span more than 40 meters with a thin concrete arch alone, whereas earlier thin arches in Switzerland had required steel cable supports.
Dvořáková's 9-centimeter concrete arches were far thinner than the arches of at least 30 centimeters that were typical of similar bridges built at the time.
Unlike the earlier thin-arch bridges built in Switzerland, Dvořáková's bridge was the first ever to span more than 40 meters using a thin concrete arch.
explanation: The goal asks for an achievement measured against one comparison group: earlier thin-arch bridges. The note that makes the bridge matter is the 'first' note, and its significance depends on the Swiss bridges, which needed cable supports. Choice B gives the first, keeps the condition that makes it a first (no cable supports), and uses 'whereas' to name the contrast with those earlier thin arches.

A.why: You picked an accurate description: the date, the designer, how thin the arches are, and the fact that the bridge is still in use. None of it says why the bridge was an achievement, and it never mentions the earlier thin-arch bridges the goal asks you to compare it with.

C.why: You saw that the significance has to be relative, but you used the wrong comparison. This choice compares the bridge with typical thick-arch bridges. The goal asks about earlier thin-arch bridges, and the Swiss bridges' arches were probably thin as well, so this contrast doesn't do the job.

D.why: You went for the 'first' and the Swiss comparison but missed that this choice drops the condition that made the bridge a first: no cable supports. The notes never say the Swiss bridges spanned less than 40 meters. Without that condition, the choice claims a record the notes don't support.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Ibarra's findings in relation to what researchers had previously assumed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Kelp forests can collapse when sea urchins overgraze them, leaving bare areas called urchin barrens.
• Researchers had long assumed that kelp returns to a barren only if urchin densities fall below about 2 per square meter.
• Marine ecologist Tomás Ibarra monitored 12 barrens off the coast of Chile for three years.
• In four barrens, kelp regrew even though urchin densities stayed above 6 per square meter.
• In those four barrens, urchins mostly sheltered in crevices and ate drifting kelp rather than grazing attached kelp.
• Ibarra concluded that urchin behavior, not just urchin numbers, can determine whether kelp recovers.
choices: Over three years, Ibarra monitored 12 urchin barrens off the coast of Chile, tracking urchin densities and recording where and how the urchins fed.
In four of the barrens Ibarra monitored, kelp regrew while urchin densities stayed above 6 per square meter and the urchins ate mostly drifting kelp.
Kelp regrew in four barrens with more than 6 urchins per square meter, well above the long-assumed threshold of 2, showing that urchin numbers play no role in recovery.
Kelp regrew in four barrens with more than 6 urchins per square meter, well above the long-assumed threshold of 2, suggesting that urchin behavior also shapes recovery.
explanation: The goal ties the findings to an earlier assumption, so the answer has to include that assumption. Regrowth at more than 6 urchins per square meter only matters because researchers expected kelp to return only below 2. Choice D sets the finding against that threshold and then states Ibarra's conclusion accurately: behavior matters as well as numbers.

A.why: You picked a description of the study's method: where Ibarra worked, for how long, and what he measured. It reports no finding and never mentions the earlier assumption, so it can't show why the results matter.

B.why: You found the key result, but here it is a bare fact. 'Above 6 per square meter' only shows significance next to the long-assumed threshold of 2, and this choice leaves that threshold out, so a reader can't tell the result overturned anything.

C.why: You correctly set the finding against the old threshold, then accepted a conclusion that goes too far. Ibarra concluded that behavior, 'not just urchin numbers,' matters. That means numbers still count. Saying they play 'no role' turns his conclusion into a stronger claim than he made.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of the fossil's age. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• For decades, paleobotanists held that broad-leaved flowering plants first appeared about 100 million years ago in tropical lowlands.
• In 2023, a team led by Ines Marrow described Velunia ternata, a fossil leaf from Chile's Karst Hollow formation.
• The leaf has the netlike veins typical of flowering plants.
• The Karst Hollow formation is about 122 million years old.
• Rocks in the formation preserve a cold upland environment.
choices: Described in 2023 by a team led by Ines Marrow, Velunia ternata is a fossil leaf with netlike veins from Chile's Karst Hollow formation.
Velunia ternata, a leaf with the netlike veins typical of flowering plants, comes from a Chilean formation about 122 million years old.
Velunia ternata, a flowering-plant leaf preserved in rocks from a cold upland, challenges the view that such plants arose in tropical lowlands.
At about 122 million years old, Velunia ternata, a flowering-plant leaf, predates by some 22 million years the time such plants were thought to have arisen.
explanation: The goal is about the age specifically. An age matters only next to a benchmark, and the first note gives that benchmark: flowering plants were thought to date from about 100 million years ago. Choice D gives the age, says the leaf is a flowering-plant leaf, and states the gap against the accepted date. That makes it the only choice that says why the age matters.

A.why: You picked an accurate description of who described the fossil, when, and where it came from. It never gives the age or says why it matters.

B.why: You saw the age and stopped there. The goal asks for its significance, and 122 million years means nothing until it is set against the 100-million-year date paleobotanists accepted. This choice leaves that comparison out.

C.why: You found a significance statement, which is the right instinct, but it is about where the leaf grew, not how old it is. Reread the goal: it asks about the fossil's age.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the achievement of Vik's plan. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Between 2015 and 2019, eleven mid-sized European cities each converted a central shopping street into a car-free plaza.
• On ten of those streets, retail sales fell for at least two years after the conversion.
• The eleventh was Marktgasse in Trelsburg, converted in 2017 under a plan led by urban planner Oda Vik.
• Vik's plan added a tram stop and set morning hours for deliveries.
• Retail sales on Marktgasse rose 9% in the first year.
choices: Vik's plan, which added a tram stop and set morning delivery hours, turned Trelsburg's Marktgasse into a car-free plaza in 2017.
Of eleven European shopping streets made car-free, only Trelsburg's Marktgasse, under Vik's plan, saw retail sales rise in the following year.
Retail sales on Trelsburg's Marktgasse rose 9% in the first year after Vik's plan made the street a car-free plaza.
Vik's plan shows that a tram stop and delivery hours guarantee rising sales whenever a shopping street becomes car-free.
explanation: The plan's achievement is relative. Its street succeeded where ten comparable streets failed. Choice B states the outcome (sales rose) and includes the comparison that makes it remarkable: it was the only one of eleven.

A.why: You picked a description of what the plan did and when. It never says the plan worked, so it states no achievement.

C.why: You found the outcome but left out the comparison. A 9% rise sounds good, but it becomes an achievement only because sales on the other ten streets fell, and this choice never mentions them.

D.why: You turned one city's result into a guarantee for every street. The notes describe one success and never show what caused it.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of the team's findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Most flu vaccines target the head of the hemagglutinin protein, which mutates quickly, so the vaccines must be reformulated every year.
• Immunologist Kenji Asaro's team asked whether antibodies to the protein's stalk, which rarely changes, could protect against many strains.
• The team gave mice an antigen made only of the stalk, then exposed them to five flu strains, each first seen in a different decade.
• None of the five strains caused illness in the vaccinated mice.
• Such protection could point toward a vaccine that need not be reformulated every year.
choices: Asaro's stalk-only antigen protected mice from five strains spanning decades, pointing toward a flu vaccine that need not change yearly.
Asaro's team gave mice an antigen made only of the hemagglutinin stalk, a part of the protein that rarely changes.
Mice given a stalk-only antigen by Asaro's team did not become ill when exposed to five flu strains from different decades.
Asaro's team showed that a stalk-based vaccine will protect people against every flu strain without ever being reformulated.
explanation: The notes follow research order, and the last note gives the interpretation: why the result matters. Choice A connects the result (protection across decades of strains) to its significance (a vaccine that might not need yearly reformulation, unlike current ones).

B.why: You picked the method. It says what the team did, not what they found or why that matters.

C.why: You stopped at the result. The finding is accurate, but the goal asks for its significance, which is that a vaccine might not need reformulating every year. This choice never says so.

D.why: You claimed far more than the notes support. The study used mice and five strains, and the notes say only that it 'could point toward' a vaccine. They don't say it will protect people against every strain.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Osei's trial in relation to earlier research. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Trials in adults have shown that bread made from iron-fortified flour reduces anemia.
• No trial had tested such flour in children under five, the age group most affected by anemia.
• In 2022, nutrition scientist Amara Osei led a trial in 40 Ghanaian villages.
• For one year, children under five in half the villages ate bread made from iron-fortified flour.
• Anemia among those children fell by 31%, compared with 4% among children in the other villages.
choices: In 2022, Amara Osei led a year-long trial in which young children in 20 Ghanaian villages ate bread made from iron-fortified flour.
In Osei's trial, anemia fell by 31% among children under five who ate iron-fortified bread, compared with 4% among other children.
Osei's was the first trial of iron-fortified flour in children under five, the group most affected by anemia, and it cut their anemia by 31%.
Osei's trial showed that iron-fortified flour reduces anemia more in young children than in adults, in every country where it is used.
explanation: The goal asks about significance relative to earlier research, so the important note is the one about the gap: no earlier trial had tested children under five, the group most affected. Choice C states that gap and the outcome that filled it.

A.why: You picked who, when, where, and what. It describes the trial accurately but never says why it matters.

B.why: You knew significance needs a comparison and found one, but it is the wrong one. Comparing with the control villages shows the result. The goal asks for a comparison with earlier research, which had never tested children under five.

D.why: The notes give no adult percentages to compare with and describe only one country, so 'more than in adults' and 'every country' both go beyond the evidence.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Fernández's findings for critics' prediction about such laws. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Pay-transparency laws require employers to include salary ranges in job postings.
• Critics argued that such laws would lower wages, since employers would anchor offers to the bottom of each range.
• Labor economist Lucía Fernández compared 300,000 job postings in Velmora from before and after its 2021 pay-transparency law.
• After the law, advertised pay rose 3% on average.
• The gap between men's and women's starting pay also narrowed by a third.
choices: Studying 300,000 job postings in Velmora, labor economist Lucía Fernández compared advertised pay before and after its 2021 law.
After Velmora's 2021 pay-transparency law, advertised pay rose 3% on average, Fernández found in a study of 300,000 postings.
Fernández found that after Velmora's pay-transparency law, the gap between men's and women's starting pay narrowed by a third.
Critics predicted that pay-transparency laws would lower wages, but Fernández found that advertised pay in Velmora rose after its law.
explanation: The goal names its own content: the critics' prediction. The finding matters because it runs against that prediction. Choice D states the prediction, gives the opposite result, and uses 'but' to make the contrast explicit.

A.why: You picked the method: who studied what. It reports no finding at all.

B.why: You found the right result but left out what makes it significant. A 3% rise matters here only because critics predicted a fall, and this choice never mentions them.

C.why: You found a striking finding, but it doesn't speak to the critics' prediction, which was about wage levels, not the gender gap. A significant result is not automatically the significance the goal asks for.

stem: The student wants to emphasize HX-4's achievement relative to existing alloys designed for extreme cold. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Most metals turn brittle at extremely low temperatures.
• Alloys that stay tough in such cold usually depend on nickel, an expensive metal.
• Materials scientist Petra Hollund's team developed HX-4, an alloy of iron, manganese, and aluminum.
• At −196°C, HX-4 kept 90% of the toughness it has at room temperature.
• HX-4's raw materials cost about one-fifth as much as those of a standard nickel-based cold-resistant alloy.
choices: HX-4, developed by Petra Hollund's team, is an alloy of iron, manganese, and aluminum that was tested at −196°C.
Unlike cold-resistant alloys that rely on costly nickel, HX-4 stays tough at −196°C with raw materials costing about a fifth as much.
Unlike most metals, which turn brittle in extreme cold, HX-4 kept 90% of its room-temperature toughness at −196°C.
HX-4 is tougher at −196°C than standard nickel-based alloys, yet its raw materials cost only a fifth as much.
explanation: The goal sets the comparison: existing cold-resistant alloys, which depend on expensive nickel. HX-4's achievement is that it matches their main property, staying tough in extreme cold, without nickel and at a fifth of the cost. Choice B states both the performance and the comparison.

A.why: You picked what the alloy is made of and who made it. It never says how HX-4 performed or why that matters.

C.why: You correctly looked for a comparison but chose the wrong one. Beating 'most metals' is something nickel alloys already do. The goal asks how HX-4 compares with alloys designed for extreme cold.

D.why: The notes never compare HX-4's toughness with a nickel alloy's, so 'tougher than' is a claim you added. The only comparison they support is cost.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Durkin's work for assessing flood risk on the Corran. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Most continuous river-flow records in the region begin after 1950.
• The Ashby Mill ledger, kept by millers, records daily water levels on the Corran River from 1781 to 1903.
• Hydrologist Maeve Durkin calibrated the ledger against a modern gauge at the same site.
• The calibrated record shows that the Corran's three largest floods all occurred before 1850.
• Current flood-risk maps for the Corran rely only on data from after 1950.
choices: Durkin's calibrated ledger shows the Corran's three largest floods all predate 1850, so flood maps built on post-1950 data omit them.
Unlike most of the region's river-flow records, which begin after 1950, Durkin's calibrated ledger reaches back to 1781.
Calibrated by Durkin, the Ashby Mill ledger shows that the Corran's three largest floods all occurred before 1850.
Durkin calibrated the Ashby Mill ledger, a millers' record of the Corran's daily water levels, against a modern gauge.
explanation: The goal asks about significance for flood risk. The work matters because the largest floods all happened before 1850, while current maps use only post-1950 data, so the maps leave out the river's worst events. Choice A connects the finding to that gap.

B.why: You saw 'earlier than others' and took it as the significance. The comparison is real, but it shows why the ledger is unusual as a record, not why it matters for flood risk. It never mentions floods or the maps.

C.why: You found the key finding but stopped short of its consequence. The pre-1850 floods matter for flood risk because current maps leave them out, and this choice never says so.

D.why: You picked the method: what the ledger is and what Durkin did to it. It gives no finding and no significance.

stem: The student wants to emphasize how Rell's discovery challenges what folklorists had assumed about the tale. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• "The Salt Bride" survives in about 60 versions collected in fishing villages along the Lirian coast.
• Folklorists assumed the tale circulated only orally until collectors first wrote it down in the 1830s.
• In 2020, archivist Tomas Rell found a sermon from 1640 that retells the tale.
• In the sermon's version, the bride returns to the sea, an ending absent from all 60 later versions.
choices: In 2020, archivist Tomas Rell found a sermon from 1640 that retells "The Salt Bride," a tale from the Lirian coast.
The 1640 sermon found by Rell ends with the bride returning to the sea, an ending absent from all 60 later versions of the tale.
Rell's 1640 sermon shows the tale was written down nearly two centuries before the 1830s, when folklorists thought it was first recorded.
Rell's sermon proves that "The Salt Bride" began as a written story and entered oral tradition only after 1640.
explanation: The assumption was about when the tale was first written down: the 1830s. The sermon's 1640 date contradicts that. Choice C gives the date, names the assumed date, and states the gap between them.

A.why: You picked who found what and when. The 1640 date is there, but without the 1830s assumption next to it, nothing tells the reader it challenges anything.

B.why: You found something genuinely unusual about the sermon. But the folklorists' assumption was about when the tale was first written down, not how it ends, so this choice doesn't challenge it.

D.why: One written retelling from 1640 does not show the tale began in writing. It may have been circulating orally well before the sermon recorded it.
